title: Anti-racism: making room for the question

turns.text: When I hear that a process may contribute to racial inequity, my first reaction can be, “But we are trying to help.” I do not want that effort to disappear from the conversation.
It does not need to disappear. We can recognize that purpose and still ask how the process works. A good intention does not answer every question about someone’s experience.
In this lesson, the team hears that families of color are less likely to return a follow-up form by the deadline. What do we actually know from that?

The example gives us a reported pattern worth examining. It does not tell us every cause. We should look at the form, mailing process, language access, and deadline, alongside the quality and limits of the information behind that report.
So “the form is the same for everyone” describes one part of the process. It does not establish that everyone has the same opportunity to complete it.
Yes. And we should not explain a racial pattern by assuming a community is less interested or less responsible. That would replace inquiry with an unsupported judgment.
How do we bring people into the conversation without asking one employee or one community partner to explain everyone’s experience?

Offer accessible ways to participate, ask about the actual task, and seek more than one perspective. A community brief can help us prepare. It is a starting point for better questions, not a description of every person.
I also see a workplace connection. If some employees get informal help and others are expected to figure a procedure out alone, that can shape assignments, feedback, and opportunities to develop.

That is another routine we can examine across the employee life cycle. We would need evidence about how opportunities are offered and experienced, including whether there is a racial pattern. We should neither assume the answer nor make race disappear from the question.
It helps to know that discomfort does not mean I have to leave the question unfinished. I can pause, notice my reaction, and return to what happened and who may be affected.

And the aim is not a confession. It is a more careful response: listen to the concern, examine the practice, and consider a change that addresses a supported barrier. You can learn privately, without sharing a colleague’s name or a personal experience.

after: Return to Priya’s decision in the existing case. Which response keeps both colleagues in the conversation while examining the form, deadline, and mailing process? Privately note what the team should investigate and one assumption it should avoid.

guidance.title: Look at what the rule does
guidance.text: A useful distinction here is between someone’s intention and the way a rule works. A deadline may be intended to make processing consistent. Yet if the notice or response route is harder for some people to use, the same deadline can create different burdens. That possibility calls for investigation. A difference in results alone does not tell us its cause. We need to examine the process and hear from people affected by it.

guidance.title: You can take a moment
guidance.text: If this raises some discomfort, you can take a moment. You do not have to decide what is in anyone’s heart. Stay with the example: what does the form ask of people, and whose experience might be missing? You can consider those questions privately. The next step is to examine a possible barrier, without jumping to a conclusion about its cause.
